messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus was forty-five years old, a chef who had spent twenty years building a career out of precision and control. He had been divorced for three years, living alone in a small apartment above the restaurant where he worked. The assault happened on a Tuesday night, after a late shift. A colleague he had trusted, someone he had trained himself, followed him into the walk-in cooler and locked the door. Marcus had not screamed. He had not fought. He had stood there, frozen, as the world he had built around himself—his kitchen, his reputation, his sense of being a man who could handle anything—collapsed into a single, unbearable moment.

In the weeks that followed, Marcus found he could talk about what happened very easily. He told his manager, he told the police, he told his ex-wife when she called to check on him. The words came out smooth and practiced, as if he were reciting a recipe. But privately, something was wrong. He could not put the memories of the event in the right order. He would recall the click of the lock, then the feel of the cold metal shelf against his back, then the sound of his own breath—but not the sequence that connected them. And every time he tried to force the memories into a timeline, he found himself pushing the memory away before he could fully recall it. It was like grabbing at smoke. His mind would skate to the edge of the image and then veer off, leaving him frustrated and hollow.

What Marcus could not shake was the feeling that he was no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. He had always been the one who could read a kitchen, anticipate every order, keep twelve stations running smoothly. Now, when a ticket came in during a rush, his hands would pause. He would stare at the paper, and a voice inside him would whisper: *You couldn't even protect yourself. What makes you think you can run a line?* He felt dirty or contaminated because of what happened, as if the walk-in cooler had left a residue on his skin that no shower could wash off. He began to believe that his life had been destroyed by the trauma. Not just altered—destroyed. The future he had imagined, the quiet pride of being a chef who had earned his place, felt like a photograph of someone else.

This belief—that he was ruined—began to shape how he remembered the event. He would start to recall the assault and, almost immediately, the memory would slip into a fog of shame. *I didn't fight. I didn't even yell.* The sequence would blur, and he would push the whole thing away, unable to hold it in his mind. The more he told himself he was contaminated, the less he could bear to let the memory surface fully. It was as if his own story had become toxic to him.

Marcus adjusted his life around this new reality. He stopped cooking at home. He stopped experimenting with new dishes. At work, he avoided the walk-in cooler entirely, sending junior staff to fetch what he needed. He stopped eating with the team after service, claiming he had paperwork to do. He began to drink more, a glass of wine that became two, then three, after every shift. His hands, once steady and quick, now trembled slightly when he plated a dish. His sous-chef noticed. His manager noticed. Marcus told them he was fine.

What finally brought him to seek help was a night three weeks ago when a ticket came in for a dish he had invented—a seared scallop with a citrus beurre blanc that had been his signature for years. He stood at the stove and could not remember the order of steps. He stared at the pan. The scallops sat in the fridge behind him, but he could not make himself turn around. He walked out of the kitchen instead, took off his apron, and sat in the alley behind the restaurant until the cold air stopped his hands from shaking.

He is afraid that if he lets himself remember the event fully, he will not survive it. He is hoping, quietly, that someone can show him how to hold it without being destroyed.
